Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch (permalink)

More than a century ago, the most powerful, wealthiest men in the world fell for a con-artist named Frederick Winslow Taylor, who sold them expensive consulting services to help them apply "Scientific Management" to their companies:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Winslow_Taylor

Upon receipt of eye-popping consulting fees, Taylor dispatched unqualified young men in "scientist" drag (lab coats, clipboards, stopwatches) to fan out over factory floors. These smart young men noted how much time each worker at each station took to perform each task, then "optimized" each worker using a homebrew choreographer's notation that showed the "correct" way to make each motion and set an upper bound for how many seconds it should take to perform each task.

Notably, these "scientists" refused to discuss their findings with the workers they observed: they never asked why a worker made a specific motion or tackled a task in a certain way. The workers were presumed to be ploddingly unreflective about their jobs (at best), or malicious featherbedders who were stealing from the boss by slacking off (at worst).

Either way, Taylor's "scientists" could see no reason to discuss their findings with the workers. The job of the "scientists" was to transform those workers into a well-oiled machine, and no one but a blockhead would ask a piston or a gear why it chose to move the way it did.

To use a technical term, these "scientists" were fucking idiots and their recommendations were (to use another technical term) bullshit. Not only did they set impossible quotas for workers, they were also notably bad at choreography and routinely required workers to move in ways that resulted in early fatigue and high rates of injury. Wherever Taylor's "scientists" went, morale plunged, labor unrest surged, and the business was made worse off.

Which all raises a question: why would the owners of these businesses – who had the intelligence and self-interest to build up extremely profitable enterprises – throw away their money and kneecap their firms on this charlatanry?

The answer lies in the psychology of Taylor's sales-pitch. Taylor's marks owed their fortunes and power to their ability to scale up their firms to sizes never before seen, thanks to innovations like the assembly line and to exogenous factors like mechanized transportation and long-distance telecommunications, which let them address much larger markets than their predecessors. The downside to this was a large workforce (too large to keep individual tabs on) that was spread out over a large factory floor or complex (too large to constantly observe).

This created a paradox: these powerful, wealthy men were vulnerable to the lowest footsoldiers in their laboring armies, any of whom might slack off, organize a union or sabotage the line, safe in the knowledge that they were part of a vast cohort that could neither be tractably surveilled nor controlled. Imagine the indignation those industrial titans must have experienced at the thought that some mere pismire could blacken their eyes and destroy their profits, and nothing could be done about it! After all, the quest for wealth and power is, above everything else, the quest for impunity, for an existence in which you can never be thwarted:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face

The Robber Barons' fury at this indignity made them easy marks for Taylor's salesmen, who promised them a return to the natural order in which workers would be literally reduced to machine-parts. After Taylor's men had done their jobs, the boss could strut the catwalks high above the factory floor and observe a visibly cowed workforce, where every worker's every moment was a constant reminder that they were there to do as they were told, not to exercise judgment, air grievances, or act in their own self-interest.

Like every power-tripping control freak, these business tyrants were their own worst enemies, doomed to a long and humiliating Tarkin's Downfall ("The more you tighten your grip, Tarkin, the more star systems will slip through your fingers" – P.L. Organa).

Taylor was no master of improving industrial production, but he was a genius at figuring out how to sell things to anxious bosses. I don't know whether Taylor believed his nonsense: he might have been every bit as satisfied as his marks at the sight of a factory full of human workers who'd been reduced to the state of machine-parts. Perhaps he truly had no inkling that the reason his services sold so well is that they played perfectly on the insecurities of business tyrants. Or maybe he was a cynic with a thorough grasp of oligarch psychology and a total indifference to the quality of workers' lives and the long-term health of his customers' business interests. Perhaps some of Taylor's executives were true believers, while others were cynics, and together they formed an unbeatable partnership because the former would go where the latter would not (and vice versa):

https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/24/supplemental-income/#andrew-tate-gwyneth-paltrow

It doesn't matter. The purpose of a system is what it does. Taylor created a template for selling garbage products to insecure bosses that made workers' lives worse and undermined the health of the firm, and that template has been mobilized by firms large and small in the years since. Every bossware company that made bank selling companies surveillance tools during the pandemic's work-from-home phase wasn't just doing Taylorism(1) (timing, surveilling and scoring workers), but also Taylorism(2) (fleecing bosses who were terrified of their workforce's power and independence):

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/02/despotism-on-demand/#virtual-whips

(In case you have any doubt, yes, this is a post about AI.)

Many workers – and even managers – have expressed bafflement at their bosses' love-affairs with AI. Even workers who can see ways to use AI tools to improve their jobs around the margins are shocked (and sometimes resentful) at their bosses' insistence that they use AI for everything, even when that adds expense and reduces quality:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/01/dare-snot/#i-will-fucking-piledrive-you-if-you-mention-ai-again

At the heart of this confusion is the fact that these same bosses are usually unwavering when it comes to measuring profit and loss and requiring a solid business-case for major shifts in corporate organization. Despite this, an AI pitchman can send these bosses swooning with all the ardor of Jensen Huang meeting an attractive woman who flirtatiously asks him to take her on a "quirky" date, say, to one of his chip warehouses?

Bosses are such easy marks for AI pitchmen for the same reason their predecessors were easy marks for Taylor's salesforce. The modern boss is a financial engineer, possibly with a law degree, whose main expertise is in balance-sheet manipulation and shareholder relations. These bosses don't know how to do anything. They can come up with as many amazing plans to revolutionize their businesses as they want, but inevitably, those plans lead to ego-shattering confrontations with skilled workers who tell them that all their ideas are impossible, illegal, or stupid:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/05/fisher-price-steering-wheel/#billionaire-solipsism

Enter the AI salesman, offering the prospect of a new workforce of literal mechanical slaves, whose presence allows the boss to fire 90% of their workers, with the result that the remaining workers will be so terrorized at the thought of losing their jobs that they never even think of sassing back:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/10/posthuman-as-in-no-humans/#hell-is-other-people

This won't work. Replacing workers with chatbots is as counterproductive as putting one of Taylor's choreographers in charge of them. Sure, AI can help workers: if the workers get to decide how the chatbots are integrated into their jobs, and if this integration doesn't increase the pace of work, making it impossible for the human workers to catch the machine's mistakes:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/05/pop-that-bubble/#u-washington

After all, the statistical methods used to produce AI outputs produce errors that are as close to being correct as is statistically possible, while still being wrong:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/06/nonfungible/#theory-free

Ergonomics are real. Taylorism is fake. Automation is real. AI is fake:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake

Statistical extrapolation tools can lead to productivity gains – just as incorporating ergonomic principles into the design of the job-site can improve productivity and reduce injury. But in both cases, the gains are contingent on the workers having a say in the deployment and a veto over demands that don't work for them.

But that's not how you sell Taylorism…or AI. The pitch isn't about making the business more profitable or efficient. Such a proposition has limited efficacy and competes against other forms of capital investment that might be better for the bottom line. The pitch is about easing the psychological trauma of being the boss but not being able to boss people around. That's an unbeatable proposition. No one will ever lose money by betting on the insecurities of America's business tyrants.

title: Gadget Review: WiFi Carbon Monoxide Alarm (JKD-625W) ★★★★⯪
content:
I was rudely woken at 5AM by the death-throes of my Carbon Monoxide alarm. Apparently it is an iron-clad law of the Universe that their dying beeps must happen while you're asleep. Right, time for a new detector as I'd rather not die of CO poisoning.

I found Smart Home Shop UK which lists items that are compatible with HomeAssistant. Their WiFi Carbon Monoxide Alarm was only £15 - which is about the same price as a non-smart one from my local ScrewFix.

This is the JKD-625W made by the OEM Symank. It comes with a backing plate, a couple of screws and rawl plugs, and a basic instruction manual. You also get three AA batteries included.

As I've mentioned before, devices with Zero Interfaces are the best. Yes, you could spend all day looking at the small LCD to count how many PPMs it is reading - but the reality is this is going to be stuck on a wall out of view. The LEDs are reasonably subtle - enough to let you know the power is working.

Pressing the test button produces a suitably loud beep. Which, basically, is all I want in an alarm.

But, of course, the real reason I bought it is the WiFi connectivity. Hold the test button for about 15 seconds, enjoy the beeping, and then it's ready to add to your network. As with any IOT device, I recommend putting it on a separate vLAN just in case it gets hacked or goes rogue.

Tuya

Like nearly all cheap smarthome devices, this doesn't have its own app or service, instead it uses Tuya. I can't complain about that, Tuya produce a reasonable Android app and seem quite happy to let HomeAssistant access their API.

Once paired the app shows some basic information about the sensor.

It's possible to create some automation routines. If it detects CO, you could switch on all the lights in the house.

The device only connects to 2.4GHz WiFi - that's fine, it isn't sending gigabytes of data and the lower frequency tends to go further, so it's fine for sticking in your loft.

One thing to note about low-power alarms like this is that they do not constantly connect to the WiFi. With only 3x AA batteries, a permanent connection would be an unacceptable power drain. So they connect once in a while to let the app know the device still exists. When the alarm sounds, they connect in order to send a push notification.

The battery is expected to last about 3 years - but the device is rated for 10 years. So factor in a few battery replacements or recharges before the decade is out.

HomeAssistant

A few seconds after I added it to my Tuya account, it automatically appeared in my HomeAssistant.

All integrated nicely. Of course, I'll have to wait for an emergency to see if it actually reports anything!

Final Thoughts

Without professional testing equipment, I'm reliant on the manufacturer's claims. But that's no different to any cheap alarm available.

For fifteen quid, it's decent. It's a small and discreet unit, the HomeAssistant integration is handy. I hope that when the battery level dips in 3 years time, I won't be woken in the middle of the night!

title: How many triangles can a graph with no pentagons have?
content:
Suppose you have a graph with n nodes and no pentagons, how many triangles can it contain?

Here a pentagon means a cycle of length 5 and a triangle means a cycle of length 3. This is an abstract property of the graph, not related to the representation of the graph on a plane, unless the graph can be embedded in a plane with no edge crossings.

A paper posted two days ago proves that the maximum number of triangles is bounded by

The notation o(1) is a term that goes to zero as n grows. See notes here.

Roughly speaking, the no-pentagon requirement takes the square root of the maximum number of triangles. The maximum number of triangles in a graph with n nodes is n(n − 1)(n − 2)/6 = O(n³) and the no-pentagon rule cuts this down to O(n3/2).

title: The Invention Algorithm
content:
As I noted in my last essay, I increasingly think that the process of creating new technologies is usefully thought of as a search process — the would-be inventor must sift through a huge mass of possibilities and pluck out from within it the specific arrangement of phenomena, parts, and components that actually performs some useful function. This is done by way of collecting and applying information about which arrangements work and which don’t, information which the inventor can use to narrow down what would otherwise be an outrageously enormous and intractable search process. When an inventor is trying to bring some new technology into the world, gathering and applying information to narrow down the space of possibilities is the primary thing that they’re doing.

But while this is useful as a high-level description, it doesn’t tell us much about what, specifically, inventors are actually doing when they’re trying to invent something. A search process implies a search algorithm — some method, or methods, that inventors are using to find working designs amidst the vast sea of potential ones. Our previous explorations of the technological search process have used random generation of possible technologies, but of course actual inventors aren’t combining elements randomly in the hopes of stumbling across something that works. To understand the nature of technological progress, it would be useful to have a sense of what algorithm our would-be inventors are using when creating some new technology, and whether some other algorithm might work better.

It’s probably not feasible to figure out the exact algorithm at work (at least, not feasible for me), since that would basically mean understanding the still-mysterious workings of the human brain. But enough histories of inventions have been written that we can draw some tentative conclusions about what sort of algorithm inventors are using.

In particular, if we look at a large number of invention case studies, we see that the first milestone is almost always the same: the would-be inventor creates some technological concept, a basic idea of the arrangement of components and phenomena that will create the desired effect.

This idea goes by different names. In patent law it’s referred to as the “inventive concept.” Thomas Edison called it the “base principle,” as did economist Brian Arthur. Soviet inventor and creator of the TRIZ method of invention Genrich Altshuller called it the “solution concept.” Engineer and professor of engineering Walter Vincenti referred to it as the “operational principle.” But regardless of what we call it, creating the technological concept is virtually always one of the very first steps when creating some new technology: once the concept is in hand, the technological search problem becomes considerably easier.

Technological concepts

Read any history of invention, and you’ll almost always find the creation of the technological concept behind it as a critical early step. The maser, for instance, began its life when physicist Charles Townes stitched the concept together while he was sitting on a park bench:

Sitting in the park, Townes took an envelope from his pocket, and worked through how such a device might work. By feeding a stream of appropriately stimulated molecules into a resonator (a cavity that would reflect electromagnetic radiation of the appropriate wavelength), any electromagnetic radiation generated within the resonator would bounce back and forth, gaining energy each time it passed through the molecules as more and more photons were generated. The device would amplify any incoming signal as an electromagnetic wave passed through the population inversion molecules. And because the resonator would reflect the wave back and forth through the molecules (a form of feedback), it could also act as an oscillator — a generator of electromagnetic signals. Power would only be limited by how quickly molecules carried energy into the resonator.

Likewise, Chester Carlson assembled the concept for what would become the Xerox machine by trawling through the scientific literature to find phenomena that could be used to copy the contents of a document:

Using finely divided powders to make visible images of electrostatic charges was an old idea in physics; it had first been done in 1777, when George Christoph Lichtenberg, a German professor, noticed that house dust adhered to an electrostatically charged piece of amber in a distinctive arrangement, which later became known as a “Lichtenberg figure.” Carlson knew about Lichtenberg figures, and Selenyi’s work reminded him of them. Suddenly, he saw that he might be able to make copies by employing a similar phenomenon in combination with photoconductivity. Instead of trying to use light to generate an electric current in a sheet of paper placed on top of a photoconductor, as he had done in his kitchen experiments, he would use light to remove electrostatic charges from the nonimage areas of a uniformly ionized photoconductor. Then he would make the pattern visible by dusting it with powder, and transfer the powder to a sheet of untreated paper.

And Paul Lauterbur came up with the concept for MRI when thinking through how the phenomenon of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) might be used to extract information from living tissue:

If you could find a way to localize the NMR signals to specific places in a patient without using harmful invasive procedures, well, that would be a different matter altogether. If physicians could do that, they could look into any part of the body remotely to see what the problem was, and the patient would be unaffected by the analysis. “I believed that NMR relaxation time measurements on tissue specimens were unlikely to contribute much to the rich variety of information available from optical microscopy. All of this information about the tissues was apparently there, however, within the living organism. Was there any way that one could tell exactly which location an NMR signal was coming from within a complex object?” That same evening he figured it out. He had taken a dinner break with Don Vickers, a friend and company officer, at a fast-food place. “On the second bite of a Big Boy hamburger,” just as he was explaining to Don that the physics of NMR precluded imaging, in midsentence, he found the principle of MRI. “I realized that inhomogeneous magnetic fields labeled signals according to their spatial coordinates, and made a leap of faith to the conclusion that the information could be recovered in the form of images.” He sketched the general idea to Don. “Heck, you could make pictures with this thing!”

We see the same thing if we look at Frank Whittle’s invention of the jet engine, or Kary Mullis’s invention of PCR, or James Watt’s invention of the separate condenser for the steam engine; in each case, the first step was the technological concept.

Technological concepts have different origins. Sometimes, like with Townes and Carlson, a concept is the product of working backward from a desired goal and gets stitched together piece by piece. Other times, they seem to appear suddenly in an inventor’s mind, such as with Tesla and his AC induction motor:

As I uttered these inspiring words the idea came like a flash of lightning and in an instant the truth was revealed. I drew with a stick on the sand the diagrams shown six years later in my address before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, and my companion understood them perfectly. The images I saw were wonderfully sharp and clear and had the solidity of metal and stone, so much so that I told him: “See my motor here; watch me reverse it.” I cannot begin to describe my emotions. Pygmalion seeing his statue come to life could not have been more deeply moved.

Sometimes concepts are the result of thinking by analogy, applying some existing technology or concept to a new domain. The idea for the Greenfield blood clot filter, for instance, was adapted from a similar filter used in oil wells, which itself was adapted from a filter to prevent people from siphoning gas out of cars:

Greenfield took his dilemma to Garman Kimmell. Kimmell, a prolific inventor, ran a company that made valves and other machinery for oil and gas wells and pipes, but he also dabbled in medical devices. As Greenfield recalls, upon hearing about pulmonary embolism, Kimmell told him, “That sounds a lot like the problem we have in the oil field with sludge.”

In oil pipelines, sludge and debris are trapped by a cone-shaped filter. The geometry of the cone, Kimmell explained, allows oil to continue flowing around its edges while concentrating the sludge in the center, whereas a flat screen, with sludge spread across it, could completely clog the pipeline. Kimmell and Greenfield decided that the conical-filter idea was worth a try in blood vessels.

Sometimes concepts are the immediate, obvious implication of some newly discovered phenomenon or material. When William Perkin accidentally created a mysterious purple chemical when trying to synthesize quinine, he immediately saw that it might be useful as a dye. Similarly, when learning about electromagnetic waves, Guglielmo Marconi immediately saw that they might be used for communication. And the discovery of X-rays by Roentgen immediately prompted people to use them for medical imaging.

A concept will often be sufficiently obvious that it will be “in the air,” and the would-be inventor will inherit it rather than come up with it themselves. The concept of the incandescent lamp is sufficiently obvious once you know that running electric current through a resistor will make it glow that it was well established decades before Edison worked on the problem. Likewise, the basic concept of a heavier-than-air flying machine was in place for nearly a century before the Wrights mounted their attempt.

Different concepts might pin down the combinations and arrangements of the elements of an invention to different degrees. Some might be rather abstract, and some might be quite specific, though they almost never pin it down so completely that no subsequent empirical searching is required. The transistor, for instance, started with what was barely a concept at all — merely the idea that some sort of solid-state phenomenon could be used to construct an electronic amplifier — and it took years of studying solid materials and how they behaved before the specific phenomena that made it possible were uncovered. The concept of the pendulum clock, by contrast — using the (nearly) constant-time swing of a pendulum as the oscillator in a clock — pinned the specifics of the invention much more tightly. Often a concept lies somewhere in the middle, providing a general idea of how an invention should work but leaving significant blank spaces in how it will be implemented. Edison, for instance, started his hunt for a practical electric lamp with the high-level concept of using electric current to heat a filament to the point of incandescence, but there were many specifics that needed to be worked out. Edison’s first implementation used a platinum filament (chosen for its resistance to oxidation) connected to a temperature regulator, specifically because he wanted to avoid dealing with vacuums. Only later did Edison modify this arrangement to eliminate the temperature regulator and use a carbon filament in a high-vacuum bulb.

More generally, while having a starting technological concept doesn’t eliminate further technological search, it does considerably narrow it. Each phenomenon selected has specific triggering conditions: to get incandescence you need some way of heating your object; to get a population inversion you need the right sort of energy combined with the right sort of material. When Edison was creating his lamp he had a huge number of possibilities to sift through — different ways to prevent the filament from burning up, different materials that might be used as a filament, different bulb atmospheres — but it was massively reduced compared to a blind search through the entirety of technology space. Similarly, any existing technology that’s used as a component can be implemented in a variety of ways, but the range of possible variation is constrained by what’s needed to make that technology work. This kind of refinement is different than needing to make a discovery of a new phenomenon, wholesale. When Frank Whittle was working on his jet engine, he needed to build new, better compressors that were far more efficient than existing ones. But he wasn’t inventing a new type of compressor working on some novel principle: Whittle’s compressor worked more or less like existing compressors did and had a very similar arrangement of elements.

We can see the effects of this search space reduction using a PTOP (Phenomena Triggered by Objects with Properties) model — a model of technology inspired by Brian Arthur’s work, where different sorts of objects, with different sorts of properties, are placed in specific arrangements to trigger various phenomena, which then modify the objects in various ways. We’ll use the simple, linear PTOP model that we looked at previously. In this model, the goal is to create an object with the highest-level triggered property (P4), by placing the right objects with the right sizes in the right order. Even with this very simple implementation — 10 object types, 10 size values, and five objects that must be chosen correctly — there are 1 billion possible options. Guessing the entire technology at once randomly requires an expected 1 billion guesses, and even randomly guessing one step at a time still requires roughly 1,300 expected guesses.

But let’s say we have a technological concept guiding our search, telling us roughly how the technology we’re searching for will work. This hypothetical concept pins down the final phenomena exactly (we know the two object types and sizes that we need), but everything else is only narrowed a bit: we know the first and third objects’ types but not their sizes, and we know that objects 1 and 2 need to be equal in size. We can see that this basic concept provides a great deal of information, significantly reducing the expected number of trials required.

This level one search is so simple that it only barely resembles the search for a real technology (even very simple technologies in the modern age have more components and potential states), but we could conduct the same exercise with a larger and more complicated PTOP model and get the same results. A concept encodes knowledge about the world and how it works, and that knowledge narrows down the range of possibilities that must be considered when building a working technology. It may not fill in the blanks completely: the would-be inventor might have no initial idea how some step in his imagined process will work. Paul Lauterbur, for instance, had to make a “leap of faith” that there would be some way to recover the magnetic field strengths of individual coordinates to turn it into pictures. And Bell’s concept for the telephone was to use a varying electric current to carry voice along a wire, but he didn’t know how to produce that current and only stumbled across a method for doing so by accident. But a concept nevertheless makes the search process far easier, bringing it from “impossible” to “tractable.”

Concepts and information

Technological concepts are, obviously, a product of our knowledge: knowledge of existing phenomena (such as the particle physics Townes used to create the concept for the maser), knowledge of existing technological elements (such as the knowledge of compressors and turbines Whittle used when creating the jet engine), and so on. This knowledge might be virtually certain, such as Edison’s knowledge of carbon’s melting point, or it might be only probable, such as the bet that there was a second histamine receptor that could be blocked by an appropriate molecule for ulcer treatment.

The knowledge that a would-be inventor has available to him acts as a sort of “palette” that he can draw from when coming up with ideas, and different inventors with different stocks of knowledge might proceed down different paths; historian Reese Jenkins notes that “[a]ny creative technologist possesses a mental set of stock solutions from which he draws in addressing problems,” (gorman and carlson 1990). Thomas Edison, for instance, repeatedly used mechanisms that he was familiar with in his inventions: Edison’s first kinetoscope used the same sort of rotating cylinder he had used in his phonograph. Likewise, in the race to build the first laser, every team attempting to build one was working off the same high-level concept but implemented it in different ways depending on their existing information endowment: the glass experts at American Optical pursued a glass laser, the gas experts at Bell Labs pursued a gas laser, ruby expert Theodore Maiman pursued a ruby laser, and so on. The more knowledge a would-be inventor has, the more possible options they have available to them, and the greater the chance they can come up with a workable concept: in the 1931 book “Industrial Creativity,” which surveyed 710 inventors on the characteristics that make for a successful inventor, “knowledge and memory” was the third most frequent characteristic noted.

When we looked at Brian Arthur’s technological evolution simulation, we noted that the key thing that made it possible to generate complex circuits randomly was modularity — combining simple elements into chunks, then making that chunk an element that could be directly manipulated and combined with other elements. Our knowledge of the world also has this basic structure: we can mentally manipulate things — concepts such as compressors, or motors, or resonant cavities — that are themselves arrangements of many individual elements, making it possible to orchestrate the arrangement of a large number of elements simultaneously.

Related to this ability to manipulate chunked information, some evidence suggests that strong mental visualization ability is an important characteristic for coming up with promising technological concepts. Inventors such as the Wright Brothers and Samuel Morse have been described as having exceptional mental visualization ability, and other notable inventors, such as Elmer Sperry, Oliver Evans, and Elihu Thomson, all described picturing a working invention in their minds before trying to build anything. Thomson stated that he “regard[ed] the imaginative faculty as chief in value to the inventor,” and that he never began a piece of work “in which I could not in my mind follow the whole thing through to an apparently satisfactory conclusion.” In “Industrial Creativity,” “imagination” was the second most frequently mentioned characteristic of successful inventors, losing out only to “perseverance.”

With mental visualization, together with the use of visual aids such as drawings, the inventor can to some extent “test” the workability of a concept, modifying it as necessary or discarding it for a new one without having to take the time and effort to build something in the real world. The Wright Brothers, for instance, initially considered a series of gears and shafts as a way to control their aircraft, but were able to foresee that its performance would be poor, and discarded it in favor of their famous wing-warping system without ever having built it. We can think of visualization as another way of processing a large number of elements at once. “A picture is worth a thousand words” is a saying for a reason: an image contains a huge number of relationships between different objects displayed that, thanks to our extensive neural machinery devoted to vision, we can process simultaneously and rapidly.

What makes a good technological concept?

We can think of a technological concept as a region in technology space that’s promising to search. A good concept is one that both has a high probability of containing a working technology and has what we might think of as an easily traversable “technological landscape” — ideally, we’d like a region that, from a given starting point (a first attempt to build a working invention), we can improve the performance of the technology rapidly in as few iterations as possible, and that allows us to reach a very high level of performance without getting trapped in local optima.

There’s probably much to be explored about what sort of technological concepts will have these sorts of characteristics, but we can venture a few guesses. One key characteristic is that we’d like our technological landscape to give us information on how we should traverse it. Specifically, if you think of “technology space” as compressed down to a 2D plane, with the third dimension, height, representing a technology’s performance, we’d like to know the slope of the landscape, so we can walk uphill: make adjustments that will yield higher and higher performance. This, of course, is how machine learning works: gradient descent via backpropagation calculates the slope of the loss landscape and then walks downhill by changing the model parameters to move in the direction of lowest loss.

This sort of technological landscape doesn’t necessarily exist automatically. In “Inventive Minds,” a book about the nature of technological creativity, Harvard professor David Perkins talks about the concept of technological “Klondike spaces”: spaces that give little to no information on the direction to proceed:

Suppose you were searching for gold in the Alaskan Klondike at the end of the nineteenth century. The governing principle of your search would have to be, “Gold is where you find it.” You would look here, there, everywhere you could. You would be persistent, try different areas, and hope for the big strike. You would know a good deal about how to look, of course. You would know what kinds of rocks might bear ore. You would have a sharp eye out for the glint of gold in river gravel. You would search upstream from sites that showed some traces, in hopes of finding the mother lode. Despite this savvy, however, you would still find that most of your time was spent in searching rather than in systematically homing in on a find.

Your search for gold is, of course, a special case of problem-solving. You are searching in the physical space of the Klondike, shifting from one position to another, exhausting dead ends, seeking new and promising terrain. Indeed, it’s useful to generalize the characteristics of this “Klondike Space,” because many other problem situations not so geological and geographical in nature have essentially the same logical topography. Many problem spaces, that is, involve punctuate targets with sharply defined boundaries (see Figure 13.1A), like a needle in a haystack or a few large nuggets or a hominid bone in a stratum. In such circumstances, it is difficult to move systematically toward a target. Rather, you find yourself casting about a lot. [My emphasis]

“Klondike spaces” are spaces where modifying a technology — making some part bigger or smaller, or faster or slower — doesn’t give obvious clues as to the direction of improvement. There are, broadly, two reasons this might occur. One is that a landscape might be highly uncorrelated — the performance of one technological option might have little relationship to adjacent options, so figuring out the local slope by making a small tweak and observing the change in performance doesn’t tell us much about which direction to head generally. When Edison was first hunting for a workable carbon filament, he found himself in this sort of landscape — he didn’t know which sort of carbon would work best, and just testing a material and seeing how long it lasted didn’t tell him much about the results he’d get from other materials, so he simply tested every type of carbon he had available to him until he found an option that was good enough.

The other reason that modifications might be uninformative is if the landscape is flat, and all nearby areas have the same performance. Consider, for instance, a string of Christmas lights where bulbs are connected in series, and every bulb needs to be working for the string to light up. If you plug the string in and it doesn’t turn on, you know that at least one bulb is burned out, but you don’t know which one, and testing one bulb doesn’t tell you anything about other bulbs or give hints as to which of them might be burned out.

An example of this sort of failure is Shockley’s first attempt to build a field-effect transistor in 1945; his theory of semiconductor behavior suggested a field-effect device should work, but extensive experiments with slightly different variations produced an effect “at least 1500 times smaller than predicted,” and he was forced to shelve the idea.

However, inventors are not simply at the mercy of these sorts of technological Klondike spaces; in practice it seems to be nearly always possible, with the proper knowledge, to determine a direction to proceed. This comes down to how we create concepts: a concept is based on some orchestration of phenomena whose behavior and triggering conditions are, to some extent, known; the individual workings of a technology can thus (in theory) be probed and experimented with to see whether the individual phenomena are behaving as expected, and give ideas as to the sort of modifications that are needed. Shockley’s failure to build a field-effect device suggested something was wrong with the existing theory of semiconductor behavior, which could then be tested and explored. Thanks in part to Shockley’s failure, it was eventually discovered that electrons trapped on the surface of a semiconductor (so-called “surface states”) were blocking the predicted field effect, a phenomenon that was then exploited to build the first point-contact transistor.

Similarly, Edison’s initial search for a carbon filament simply tested every carbon material that happened to be available, but careful examination of the materials tested suggested that materials that consisted of many parallel fibers performed the best — Edison later stated that paper was useless as a filament material because under a microscope it looked like “a bunch of sticks thrown together.” This initial search was followed then by a second, more thorough search that was focused specifically on fibrous carbon materials, leading to the bamboo filament.

This, I think, is one of the key things that technological concepts, and the knowledge that underlies them, do for the technological search process: they mean that the would-be inventor is never trapped in a Klondike space, and with the proper information and experiments can nearly always figure out a promising search direction.

We can similarly make some tentative conclusions about the sorts of technological concepts that might be improved upon rapidly, in as few iterations as possible. Something that has been demonstrated repeatedly is that the more modular the design of a technology is, the easier it is to improve rapidly. McNerney et al. 2011, for instance, used simulations to show that technologies with a greater degree of connectivity between components — the more the performance of one element was a function of other elements — had shallower learning curves and a slower rate of improvement compared to technologies with less connectivity.

But the most thorough demonstration of this effect I’m aware of is Stuart Kauffman’s NK model, developed to model fitness landscapes in evolution. In the NK model there are two parameters: N, which is the number of genes in some genome, and K, which is how much each gene’s fitness contribution depends on other genes. When K is 0, every gene contributes to fitness independently; if genes can have either a “good version” with a value of 1 and a “bad version” with a value of 0, overall fitness is just the sum of every gene’s value. But if K is 1, then the fitness of each gene depends on the value of one other gene; if K is 2 it depends on two other genes, and so on.

Increasing K increases the ruggedness of the fitness landscape. When K is 0, the landscape is smooth, there’s a single peak of maximum fitness, and it’s easy for evolution to walk up the hill to reach it. When K is very high, the landscape becomes, according to Kauffman, like “the surface of the moon,” there are a huge number of local optima, and finding the peak becomes very slow. From “At Home in the Universe”:

As the density of interconnections increases, changing a single gene (or bit in the program) will have effects that ripple throughout the system. It will be difficult indeed for it to smoothly evolve, with slight changes in the genome making correspondingly slight changes in fitness. So putting the effects together, as K increases, the heights of the peaks decrease, their numbers increase, and evolving over the landscape becomes more difficult.

We can demonstrate these same benefits of modularity with a PTOP model. The technology below is made up of 25 objects, arranged in five modules; each group of objects triggers its own series of phenomena, which modifies a different property in the final, output object. The goal of the technology is to maximize the product of all five output phenomena, which is achieved by dialing in the proper size for each object.

This implementation of the technology is highly modular; there’s little connectivity between the various objects/phenomena, and finding the maximum possible performance is relatively quick. This is the equivalent of a very low value of K in Kauffman’s NK model.

We can increase “K” by changing the nature of phenomena. In the model below, phenomena have a 40% chance to depend on the properties of multiple input objects, not just one, and these extra connections can be between any predecessor object, including ones in different modules. This makes it harder to find the best possible design, because hill-climbs now get stuck on local peaks. And the greater the degree of connectivity, the smaller the chance that the best design gets found. While in the unconnected version you could dial in each object’s size independently (smoothly climbing up the single peak), that doesn’t work when you start adding connections: you can’t simply dial in the optimum value at one spot and then move on to the next one.

So modularity doesn’t just make it easier to find working arrangements in technology space — it makes improving the performance of a technology far faster and easier.

What sort of algorithm should we use to find concepts?

Creating the concept is only the first milestone in the technological search process, and it’s my impression that it’s not a particularly binding step — if it was, I think we’d see a lot more inventions that could have been invented far earlier than we do. But it would nevertheless be useful if we could create technological concepts that reliably contained workable technologies capable of a high degree of performance. How might we go about this?

There have been various suggestions for these sorts of “invention algorithms.” One such algorithm has been suggested by Ed Boyden, neuroscientist and co-inventor of expansion microscopy and optogenetics. Boyden calls his method the “tiling tree”: break the problem down into the elements that it needs to contain and think of every possible way of doing each of them:

With optogenetics, my co-inventor Karl Deisseroth and I — when we were both students, we just started going through all the laws of physics. How would you control the brain? Well, there’s only so many kinds of energy. There’s mechanical force. There’s magnetism. There’s light. The list is pretty short, actually. You can actually try to write down every possible way of doing it. I call this method the tiling tree method, where you try to take this base of possibilities and break it down into parts.

If you draw it properly, it looks like a tree diagram. Here’s this base of possibilities split into two parts, and each of those splits into more parts, and eventually it covers a page. It looks like a tree, and then the leaves of the tree — the bottom nodes — are ideas you could actually test by doing a literature search or doing an experiment. A lot of our projects, actually, at some point or another involve this kind of can-we-think-of-every-possible-idea approach.

Boyden points to Fritz Zwicky, a 20th-century astronomer, as the originator of this concept, who dubbed it “morphological analysis.” Here, for instance, is a chart showing a partial morphological analysis of different sorts of telescopes you might build:

In Zwicky’s version, the result is a “morphological box” — a multidimensional box where each axis is one category of variation the technology could have. So in the example above, you could have “unmanned, balloon-mounted neutrino detectors,” or “moon-based gamma ray telescopes that send telemetrics back to earth.” The goal of this sort of algorithm is to systematically list the different possibilities, letting you come up with concepts that you otherwise might have missed.

But the most developed method I’m aware of for coming up with technological concepts is called “TRIZ.” TRIZ, which is an acronym for “Theory of Inventive Problem Solving” in Russian, was created by Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller in the second half of the 20th century. In the 1940s, Altshuller was in the Soviet Army working as an “invention inspector” and was tasked with helping inventors prepare patent applications and solve various problems related to invention. Having no good method for helping inventors with their problems, Altshuller eventually created one.

I would classify TRIZ as a sort of industrial improvement system, like Lean or Six Sigma or scientific management, with all that the designation implies. Having spent a lot of time studying industrial improvement systems, I think that they’re almost always based around some core insight or insights that are correct and useful. But they tend to put too little emphasis on building the intellectual foundations around these insights, and the insight tends to get applied in a “when you have a hammer everything looks like a nail” sort of fashion; practitioners are quick to take the insight out of its original domain and try to apply it as broadly as possible. Literature on industrial improvement systems tends to have “salesman energy,” implying the ability to solve all your problems with one weird trick. It’s often targeted at managers or other nontechnical people (and thus written in a less-than-rigorous way), and is often extolled by a sort of cadre of consultant-types that collects around the system, selling books and courses and offering cringey-sounding certifications. (So just as you can be a black belt in Six Sigma, you can earn the title of TRIZ Master.) In my experience there’s often value in extracting the actual valuable information embedded within industrial improvement systems from the consultant slop that accretes around them — my book “The Origins of Efficiency” is in some ways one big exercise in doing this — and I suspect TRIZ is similar.

TRIZ is, essentially, based around the idea of technological search. Altshuller breaks new inventions down into five categories, based on how difficult the search process is for coming up with the idea for them. Level 1 inventions require simply small variations of an existing idea and can be discovered easily after a few trials. Level 2 inventions are slightly more complex and might require 10 to 100 different ideas before an engineer discovers a workable concept. At level 5, the most complex, the unaided inventor might require 10 to 100,000 trials, or perhaps might never discover a workable concept, because it requires a fundamentally new phenomenon that the inventor isn’t aware of. The greater the level of invention, the greater the knowledge needed to find a good concept.

The basic thesis of TRIZ is that by default people do not search for concepts very efficiently; they try different arrangements of elements based on their own experience or simply try and combine ideas by pure trial and error in the hopes they might work. This sort of search process might work for the simplest level 1 and level 2 inventions, but it’s inappropriate for the more transformative inventions of the higher levels. TRIZ is in large part devoted to getting people to think in new ways to come up with more promising concepts, sort of in the tradition of brainstorming or Oblique Strategies. Altshuller notes Zwicky’s morphological analysis as a way to generate new concepts that’s better than people’s default methods, but thinks it’s insufficient in part for combinatorial explosion reasons: the more axes of possibility you add, the more possible options you must consider, and the number of variants quickly gets enormous. An invention with merely mid-level difficulties, Altshuller notes, might have millions of possible variations to consider.

Instead of enumerating all possible concepts, TRIZ focuses on using tools to come up with better concepts. The heart of this is what’s known as a “technical contradiction.” Per Altshuller, the fundamental difficulty in coming up with a good technological concept is conflicting requirements: increasing performance along one axis might require raising some value, while increasing it along another axis might require lowering it. For an airplane, getting it into the air is aided by decreasing the weight, but making it strong enough to withstand the forces subjected to it is aided by increasing the weight. In Altshuller’s view, the creation of a new invention fundamentally requires some way of overcoming this contradiction, so you don’t have to sacrifice one measure of performance for another.

To overcome these technical contradictions, TRIZ provides several tools, chief of which is its list of 40 principles: a list of heuristics for how to rearrange the elements of a concept to eliminate the technical contradiction. Principles are things like “segmentation — divide an object into independent parts,” “prior counteraction — preload countertension to an object to compensate for excessive and undesirable stress,” and “asymmetry — replace symmetrical forms with asymmetrical forms.” These principles are, supposedly, based on analysis of tens of thousands of patents to determine what technical contradictions are encountered in practice and what methods can be used to overcome them. There’s an involved algorithm for applying these principles called ARIZ, but in essence a would-be inventor first imagines the most perfect, ideal version of an invention, a North Star to navigate by. He then determines the technical contradiction at work preventing him from achieving the ideal version of the invention and consults a “contradiction matrix,” which states which principles might be applied to resolve it. Properly applied, this results in the generation of a better concept that pushes an invention toward its ideal state.

I don’t necessarily think TRIZ holds the key to understanding the nature of invention; like with any industrial improvement system, I think it’s probably a mix of valuable ideas, exaggerated benefits, and consultant drivel. But I suspect there’s some promising work that could be done by analyzing the various elements of TRIZ — the ARIZ algorithm, the contradiction matrix, the list of principles, and so on — to try and understand more about the nature of technology space and how it might be searched effectively.

For instance, many TRIZ principles suggest pushing some particular parameter higher or lower: making air more reactive (principle 38) or less reactive (principle 39), changing the degree of feedback (principle 23), amplifying a harmful factor (principle 22), and so on. (In fact, principle 35 is just a bunch of parameters you might try changing.) This reminded me of a bit from Richard Hamming’s “The Art of Doing Science and Engineering,” where he notes that in high-dimensional spaces, almost all the mass of an object is concentrated near the surface, which suggests that for any given design of an object the optimal design will have some particular parameter pushed as far as it can go.

Similarly, one of the steps in one version of the ARIZ algorithm is applying the “size time cost” heuristic — imagining the invention with size, time, and cost pushed either toward zero (as small as possible, a process as fast as possible, or a cost as cheap as possible) or toward infinity, and imagining what the solution looks like under these modified constraints. This is a specific example of a more general idea, expressed in Judea Pearl’s book on problem-solving heuristics, that search heuristics are often developed by thinking of ways to solve simplified versions of the problem (such as problems with various constraints eliminated or added).

Conclusion

The first milestone in creating some new technology is the creation of the technological concept: some basic idea of what arrangements of phenomena and objects will, together, create a working technology. This doesn’t eliminate the search problem — many of the most famous inventors, such as the Wright Brothers and Thomas Edison, faced most of their difficulties once the concept was in place. But the concept transforms what would be an impossibly difficult search problem into one that’s far more tractable.
description: As I noted in my last essay, I increasingly think that the process of creating new technologies is usefully thought of as a search process — the would-be inventor must sift through a huge mass of possibilities and pluck out from within it the specific arrangement of phenomena, parts, and components that actually performs some useful function.

title: AI researchers debate what we should do next – Daniel Kokotajlo and Ege Erdil
content:
New podcast episode between Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. I thought this was going to be a debate, but they ended up agreeing on a lot more than I expected.

Their main point of disagreement is how likely it is that we get some intelligence explosion that gives us AIs more competent than any human expert before 2029. Ege puts this possibility at around 20%, whereas Daniel thinks it’s higher than 50%.

They agree that there is not a huge difference in probability, and that, in either case, the situation is crazy enough that our civilization really needs to grapple with how the world might be transformed, and we need a plan that actually makes sense.

In particular, we should stop antagonizing China if we think some kind of global treaty will be needed to make superintelligence go well.

There was another important crux about how well we should expect future AIs (that swamp humans in population size and cognitive power) to treat us, and how relevant it is that current AIs, by and large, seem to be pretty nice.

We close off with predictions for 2027. Daniel, of course, expects superintelligence next year. Ege’s median for full automation is 2040, but by next year he expects AIs that can beat any video game on Steam, and which can control robots to get simple physical tasks (like folding laundry) done at roughly human speed.

Transcript

0:00:00 – Will we have superintelligence by 2029?

Dwarkesh Patel

Today, I’m joined by Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. Ege is a researcher at Google DeepMind. Daniel is one of the authors at the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027 and AI 2040.

I wouldn’t call this exactly a debate, because I hope it’ll be more of a discussion. But there is a set of key disagreements you guys have, which leads one of you, Daniel, to believe that AI is likely to kill us all within the next few years, and Ege, you to believe that will not happen. I feel like a big crux in this conversation is just timelines. How soon do you expect extreme superintelligence?

I’ve articulated, and Paul has articulated in the last episode, why there could be extreme superintelligence soon. Ege, why do you think that’s unlikely?

Ege Erdil

The main difference between me and Daniel, and also between me and Paul, is just how much you believe in the software-only singularity.

This is the idea that you have a fixed pool of compute and a roughly fixed amount of data that is at least not synthetic. Then what happens is that you get better AIs. That’s what it will look like when we have these robots. It won’t be that we suddenly have robots and we have this industrial explosion that suddenly takes off. It will initially be that there are some tasks we can automate using these models that we couldn’t do before because our robots were too stupid. But we won’t get a situation in which we are getting an industrial explosion, because there will still be human bottlenecks in management and telling the systems what to do.

Dwarkesh Patel

I guess the way we’ve seen automation in other sectors, it does seem to me that you get a glimmer of coding ability, and then you get swamped by coding ability. It’s not like you get 5% on SWE-bench, and the year after you get 10%, and then 15%, and 20%, and then there’s this exponential decrease…

Ege Erdil

That’s not the way I would put it, though. We have seen a longer tail across skills. What you’re saying is correct for any one skill that you can measure. But what I just expect is that there will be more skills of this kind. For example, let’s say you get robots, but they’re unable to do continual learning or something. That’s probably what happens, actually.

Daniel Kokotajlo

I totally agree with you that if we do the superintelligence-first thing and then do the robots, then it will hit us like a truck. But if we instead do robots in the ordinary way, then for some period of time, they will be exactly like you describe, where they can do a specific task if you tell them to. But if you give them a more ambitious, longer task, like keeping the house clean or something, then they’ll get stuck or flail around.

But I would apply the concept of horizon lengths here and say that probably, just like with many other types of tasks, they would start off like that, but then the horizon length of tasks that they can autonomously do would double twice a year or double three times a year.

Then it seems hard to get 15 years if that’s what you’re doing, because even after just the first three years, you’re getting 100x improvement in horizon length. So it seems to me that if you think that by the end of 2027, the AIs will be able to do dishes or fold laundry when someone tells them to, then by 2030, they should be able to just manage the house or something.

Ege Erdil

I’m not sure. The concept of horizon length seems like too much of a leaky abstraction to me here. When I use agents for coding stuff, there are tasks which would take a human many weeks that they can do. But there are other tasks that would take a human 10 minutes that they can’t do. Often it’s not even easy to understand how these tasks are distributed.

A task can look extremely technically complicated and ambitious: take this program and completely formalize it and prove things about it or whatever. This is the kind of thing a human would take many months on. An agent can often do it in hours.

While a much simpler task like, “I’m going to put you in charge of looking at other people’s changes to this codebase, and make sure you don’t approve something if it looks obviously dumb or if it breaks something,” this kind of thing, they just can’t retain memory. They can’t understand what it means for something to be bad or dangerous to merge.

It’s because there’s too much context. They are bad at arranging information in such a way that they retain all the context, they know what’s relevant and what’s not relevant. There seems to be something missing there, and it’s causing their horizon lengths to be extremely jagged.

On the tasks which are of the second type that I’m talking about, I don’t think we’ve been seeing progress that is 10x a year in horizon length.

Daniel Kokotajlo

This is a live question for me. This is something that’s somewhat crux-y for me. If I were more convinced that they were really not improving that much at a whole range of really important skills, that would lengthen my timelines significantly.

One question I have is, how much hard evidence do we have that this is the case versus just anecdotes? A skeptical-of-this-hypothesis but more bullish hypothesis overall about AI would be that, at any given level of AI capability, there will still be things that they still can’t do. As you give your AIs more ambitious tasks, you’ll still notice that they’re failing at this sort of thing.

You’ll constantly be running up against their failures. That might give the misleading impression that they’re not really improving that much, even if the things that they’re failing at are more impressive than the things they were failing at two years ago.

Basically, one thought is, how confident are you that they really aren’t improving that much over the years, versus they are improving a lot, it’s just that there’s a significant order of magnitude or two gap?

Ege Erdil

It’s difficult to name a task where the AIs are not making significant progress, just in capability. That was not true, I think, some number of years ago, but right now it is true.

The difference here is more, do you think the progress in some metric, let’s say horizon lengths or something like that, is 2-3x a year, or is it more like 10x or 100x a year? It’s more a quantitative question as opposed to, are they making progress or not?

For example, in the skill of writing an original novel that is good, I think the progress since last year is definitely not 100x. Probably not even 10x. It might be 3x, but this is very subjective. It’s very hard to measure this.

But with a lot of these things, we don’t have anything like METR’s time horizon benchmark to settle these questions. I’m just having to make these intuitive judgments because we don’t have good benchmarks. So I could be totally wrong about some of this, and if you were to quantify it, it will come out that I was wrong.

With the time horizon thing, I think the issue is that the moment you turn it into a benchmark, it has to be something that the AIs can already do reasonably well enough, that can then become an optimization target, and that makes it relatively easy to make progress on it.

My guess of what would happen for the METR time horizons thing, and I’ve said this, I think, early last year, was that this is basically going to diverge. They’re going to get near infinite time horizon. But there will still be a bunch of just 10-minute tasks that the AIs can’t actually do very well because of just distributional shift. That has basically happened now. They stopped reporting the numbers because it was diverging.

But take some domain in which they can do a 10-minute task now. What is the length of the task that they will be able to do in that domain in one or two or three years? It’s probably just very domain sensitive. So I don’t really have a very good answer to this question, because we don’t have a good benchmark that can settle it.

It’s just my intuitive judgment, based on using the systems, that they seem like they made vast progress in math, probably even more than 100x in terms of time horizon over the last year. In some other domain — like sending emails on my behalf that are not confusing and that people on the other side can understand — I feel like the progress is much, much less.

Dwarkesh Patel

I’ll give you a concrete example. For many years, I have been asking any AI CEO who comes on my podcast how soon before they can automate being a video editor for my podcast. The time horizon on that has maybe doubled over the last year and a half or something.

But if I give Fable a transcript of my podcast and I’m like, “How should this be reorganized to be more coherent?” It’s just not clear that there’s been that much progress from Claude 3.7.

Ege Erdil

Yeah, I think that matches my qualitative impression. But I thought when I was using the models that there was a pretty big leap in, for example, writing quality with 3.6 Sonnet. It felt like the first model I could actually use to try to write stories and fiction. It actually would be decent if a human was managing it.

In the current state we’re at, they can write somewhat longer things, but definitely not 100x longer without it becoming bad. I agree, Dwarkesh, that the effective time horizon, maybe that would be more than 2x over the last 1.5 years, but it’s not more than 10x over the last 1.5 years. But it’s very subjective. This is some evidence for the fact that this rate of progress is incredibly jagged. In math, since two years ago, it’s one million times or something. You can make that case. Some ridiculously high number.

1:23:38 – Is AI research actually verifiable?

Daniel Kokotajlo

I think this is plausible. My follow-up question then is, to what extent can this be explained by the training environments? I would imagine that they have a lot of training environments that are of the form, “Prove this theorem or disprove this theorem,” and a lot of training environments that are of the form, “Solve this coding problem,” or, “Write this piece of software that passes these unit tests.” And not many problems that are of the form, “Make a good aesthetic judgment about how to organize clips” or something like that, because it’s harder to set up that sort of environment, and maybe also because it’s less lucrative, although I’m not sure about that.

You work at DeepMind, so do you think that a lot of this jaggedness is basically downstream of just the task distribution? Or do you think that it’s like, “Oh no, I’ve seen examples of the company trying really hard to collect a lot of high-quality data and training environments for a particular type of 10-minute task such as that, and then just still failing to get the AI as good at it”?

Ege Erdil

I can’t speak to what the company is doing internally. What I can say is based on just public evidence. There’s a cost to verification that I think is driving a lot of this.

I don’t really agree with the split that some tasks are verifiable and some tasks are not verifiable. For example, did you produce a video for his podcast that will make Dwarkesh happy? That’s verifiable. You can give the video to him, and he’s like, “What the hell is that?” But the issue is that’s a very expensive way to get feedback.

The difference with math is that math is very cheap to get feedback on. There’s a very cheap verifier. That does have a huge effect, because the way you should think about it is: how efficiently can you sample trajectories that give you the right answer? How fast can you discriminate things that work from those that don’t work? That’s a very fundamental thing for how efficiently you can learn things.

One thing, for example, that makes me more skeptical of software-only singularity type stories is that while I agree that ML research is a verifiable domain, in practice a lot of the verification is quite expensive. This is why compute matters so much. That’s why compute is so important for algorithmic progress.

You can have innovations at small scales that fail at large scales. You can have innovations that only work at large scales that you can never confirm by experiments at small scales because they just completely fail. You get false positives and false negatives in both directions. If you want to collect a bunch of data about this to train the models to have better taste, that needs a lot of compute as well, and probably more and more as you scale up the size of the experiments.

That makes me not put as much credit on the arguments that say, “Look, we made a decade of progress in one or two months in math, and therefore we should expect a decade of progress in ML research.” If you think of the dollar cost of verifying some idea in ML research and compare it to the dollar cost of verifying a math proof, it’s many, many orders of magnitude apart.

Seeing if some proof of the Riemann hypothesis in Lean is correct or not, you can do that on your personal computer. It’s very easy. There’s a linear time algorithm for checking proofs, basically. While if you’re trying to figure out, “I have this fancy change to this optimizer, does that really give me a compute efficiency when I’m pre-training or not?”, it’s very hard to settle that question. You can do small-scale experiments. It can look like it works, but then you scale it up and, “Oh wait, it doesn’t work. What’s going on?” Then it’s very confusing.

To me, it looks like the cost of verification is much, much higher. That’s probably, honestly, a key reason to expect that domain to be significantly more difficult to automate. It’s not that humans are very good at it, because I think humans are also bad at ML research, just like we’re bad at math.

It’s just that AIs, due to their current sample inefficiency and stuff like that, really benefit from being able to get just a ton of data in there. That is very contingent on there being a very cheap verification procedure for whether you did the right thing or not. The more expensive that is, the slower you make progress, basically. So that’s my rough take about this.

Dwarkesh Patel

There is some argument about generalization with respect to the cost. Even in math, presumably the way that these models became good at, say, being able to accommodate billions of tokens — or was it hundreds of millions of tokens — in order to solve Navier-Stokes across a swarm of thousands of agents was not through many other tasks where 1,000 agents collaborated in order to solve a math proof and spent tens of millions of dollars’ worth of tokens to do so. There was some generalization to a much more ambitious kind of assignment from the math training that they underwent.

Then the question is, will you see that kind of generalization in AI research? Now, of course, they’re much more sample efficient than humans, so you can’t use this as an exact analogy.

But my understanding is that researchers who were in the field in, say, 2020, when there was much less compute being used, at a level of compute that can be part of the training process now, are good at doing AI research now. There are some lessons they learned from training GPT-2- or GPT-3-size models that are helping them do good research at the current frontier. So it does seem like you should expect to see this kind of generalization.

I agree that you could not cheaply and consistently verify at the scale at which you’d need the AI researchers operating.

Ege Erdil

I totally agree with that. You should expect to see a lot of generalization. In fact, we have seen a lot of generalization, as you said, just based on Navier-Stokes.

The other thing I would say is that there is such a thing as general intelligence. With these base models, I think pre-training loss is a pretty good proxy for that thing. It does just predict, in a bunch of ways, “Will the model understand some subtlety about your request and interpret it correctly even though it was ambiguous?” and all kinds of things we normally associate with intelligence. It just does predict it.

Obviously the entire reason this field works at all is because this concept exists. Otherwise this wouldn’t work. I totally agree with that. For example, there was this plot that was published by Anthropic about pre-training compute multiplier sizes or something like that. They didn’t report actual sizes, but there was a plot published in their IPO roadshow.

I have some difficulty interpreting that plot. I can’t exactly say what I think is wrong with it. I think they’re not disclosing a lot of information that is relevant for thinking about whether you trust their judgment of what’s going on or not. I can say, based on the information I have, that I don’t trust their judgment of what’s going on, but I can’t explain why. That’s a little bit unsatisfying.

Daniel Kokotajlo

Does that mean you think that there hasn’t been an acceleration in pre-training progress over the last year at Anthropic?

Ege Erdil

I would say that question is poorly posed. I don’t think I can elaborate more than that without revealing something. You can say there has been and there hasn’t. It depends on how you interpret the question.

Dwarkesh Patel

Interesting. I’ll put that in Claude and see what it thinks.

Daniel Kokotajlo

It’s an update to hear that you don’t believe it. So that’s something.

Ege Erdil

I’m not saying I don’t believe it. I’m saying the thing they are reporting is poorly posed. I’m not saying they made up the numbers. I think there is a real graph inside Anthropic that probably looks like that. They didn’t fabricate the numbers. It’s just that I think that doesn’t mean what they are portraying it to mean.

Dwarkesh Patel

I’m guessing what you’re referring to is that there’s some synthetic-data-type compute multiplier that makes it look like the loss on that corpus is higher, but maybe in a way that doesn’t generalize. Of course, I can only speculate, but these are the kinds of things one could think make the pre-training thing misleading.

Ege Erdil

I can’t comment on that. But this is a trade-off. This is something people have to decide. You can decide people should be more transparent. You can have a regulation that companies have to be more transparent, they have to publish a bunch of information. But then you have to accept the fact that anything that is published, China also finds out.

Dwarkesh Patel

Well, China’s finding out anyways. At least we get to find out.

Daniel Kokotajlo

Yeah, I accept that fact. They’re probably finding out anyway.

Ege Erdil

Right now, there’s a lot of leakage because security posture is so bad. But in a world where you also want to improve the security posture, doing both of these interventions at once defeats a lot of the point of improving security, if you’re also going to get the labs to publish all of this information anyway.

Maybe you can defend the weights, and the weights are not going to get stolen. But basically everything else, all the algorithmic innovations and so on, they would very easily just reconstruct from the public information. That is a cost. It might be a cost worth paying, depending on how dire you think the situation is in a bunch of ways.

Daniel Kokotajlo

I think it is worth paying.

Ege Erdil

But then the proper way to do that… Again, that’s why I think improving the quality of public discourse, not about these specific details, but just about the general fact of the transformativeness of the technology and the size of the impact it will have, is so important. If the public takes this seriously, then this is a decision that could be made by the government. Then it could become a regulation. We could just accept that, “Yes, we understand there’s a cost here, but given the stakes of the situation, we think we should pay this cost.”

For example, Anthropic doesn’t believe that. Even though they also are aware of the stakes, they just don’t think that cost is worth paying. I think that’s what’s going on. I don’t think they’re necessarily being self-interested about that. They just have a real belief that this would be worse for the world if they made that information public. But Daniel doesn’t share that belief.

If there’s no public discourse about it, it’s impossible to get the companies to actually publish this stuff. There has to be some external thing that comes in and says, “Look, you guys can think that, but we are aware of the stakes here. We have decided that it is important for this information to be public.” Unless that can happen, anyone can say, “Look, I think it’s better for the world, and I’m just going to do what I think is best.” There’s no regulation, there are no rules.

That’s a very bad situation. Not because I necessarily think that the decision to keep it secret is a wrong decision, but because the process that’s outputting that outcome is bad. As I said, there should be a plan. We should understand what the stakes are. There should be rational public deliberation about this topic, and people should come to a conclusion: “Yes, we want this,” or, “No, we don’t want this.” That has not happened at all.

This is a unilateral decision that is being taken by some people who might be right, might be wrong. They have certain preferences. Even the government, I think, is not really playing a large role in that, because they don’t understand the stakes.

The government might play a role in something like, “Oh, we are worried about Chinese cyber attacks, and we want to have capable cyber models. We don’t want that to get leaked.” Or they might worry about specific concrete risks. But if you don’t appreciate the total transformative potential of the technology, that it’s going to totally change the human condition, for example, then you’re just unaware of the stakes. You’re not going to make the right decisions.

Dwarkesh Patel

This was a very productive discussion. I feel it was very helpful to iron out what the cruxes were within the context of people who take the potential of this technology seriously. Thanks, guys.

Daniel Kokotajlo

Thank you.
